exhibit0.label: Exhibit 0
exhibit0.question: What does "the best interface is the one you forget exists" mean to you as someone who builds systems?

custody.status: Output matches Flow history word for word
custody.note: "As I said it" is my own hand transcription of what I said, typed from my voice memo.

takes.label: Take 1
takes.raw:
Okay, so... the best interface... I think it's basically when you don't have to think about using it, like learning it sorry sorry how to use it.

Like, when you're using something and you're not constantly wondering where to click or what to do next.

You're just... doing what you came there to do.

And, yeah, I think that's actually quite difficult to build. Because all the complicated stuff, the logic, the decisions... someone has to handle all of that. Just not the user.
takes.output: Okay the best interface, I think, is basically when you don't have to think about how to use it, like when you are using something and you are not constantly wondering where to click or what to do next. You are just doing what you came there to do. I think that's actually quite difficult to build because all the complicated stuff, the logic, the decisions, someone has to handle all of that, just not the user.

takes.label: Take 2
takes.raw:
Wait, I think there's another way to look at this.

We spend so much time learning how to use technology... remembering commands, figuring out buttons, changing ourselves to fit the tool adjusting to how a tool works.

But why? I mean, shouldn't it be the other way around?

Shouldn't the technology adapt to how we naturally think and communicate?

Because we already know what we want to say. We shouldn't have to learn the tool first struggle just to get it out.
takes.output: I think there's another way to look at this. We spend so much time learning how to use technology: remembering commands, figuring out buttons, adjusting to how a tool works. But why? Shouldn't it be the other way around? Shouldn't the technology adapt to how we naturally think and communicate? Because we already know what we want to say, we shouldn't have to struggle just to get it out.

boundary.yLabel: Index speedup over full scan (log scale)

points.label: 1 symbol: 40.6x less CPU than a full scan

boundary.note: Nasdaq ITCH sample of 268,744,780 messages plus synthetic workloads. One machine, one workload. The crossover point was not measured here.

contamination.note: A second agent session competed on the pinned core in 9 of 10 rounds. A second run broke the predeclared quiet-machine threshold. Both were rejected for invalid conditions, and a later run was accepted.

chips.text: 26 findings, then 14 more; fixes recorded in project docs, not independently rerun

call.question: TipIndex's index used 40.6x less CPU than scanning everything when you follow one symbol. What happens when you follow 1,000 symbols?
options: It becomes slower than a full scan
call.reveal: At 1,000 symbols the index lost. I published both regimes, so you can see where it stops being true.

cases.title: A project built to prevent looking into the future did exactly that
cases.what: Tests found a daylight-saving fold that could admit a future event at an earlier cutoff; duplicate keys and chunk boundaries could give wrong AS OF answers.
cases.resolution: Found, fixed and resolved before the resume claim.

cases.title: A headline benchmark did not survive a clean rerun
cases.what: One headline number lacked a clean reproducible provenance; a cache-line-layout advantage fell from about 3.1x to about 1.02x on rerun.
cases.resolution: Published the slower, defensible numbers and reclassified the inconclusive improvement.

cases.title: 324 tests passed, then a 19-finding audit
cases.what: A separate forensic audit found 19 issues the tests never asked about, including quadratic CPU on an overlong email, response amplification and starvation.
cases.resolution: Regression test per finding, caps, fairness, tokens. No blanket security guarantee.

cases.title: I rejected my own benchmark runs
cases.what: Another agent session competed on the pinned core in 9 of 10 rounds; a second run broke the predeclared quiet-machine threshold.
cases.resolution: Both rejected for invalid conditions, not for bad-looking numbers. A later run was accepted.

cases.title: The watchdog called a dead connection healthy
cases.what: A late heartbeat reply could restore HEALTHY.
cases.resolution: Late replies are now rejected as liveness; tests added with the simulator.

cases.title: The index was 40.6x better, until it was worse
cases.what: One symbol: 40.6x less CPU than a full scan. At 1,000 symbols the index lost.
cases.resolution: Published both regimes and the boundary instead of claiming one universal winner.

cases.title: I built an extra feature, then did not merge it
cases.what: An optional QR verification route was built on a branch and failed a required test I had declared in advance.
cases.resolution: Not merged. The old test contract may have been too rigid; that is noted openly.

cases.title: The comparison was unfair because every thread was pinned to one core
cases.what: Every spawned thread inherited CPU 0 pinning, which overstated the epoll versus thread-per-connection difference.
cases.resolution: Reset affinity, report per-thread CPU, interleave trials.

cases.title: The polling budget: better tail latency, more total work
cases.what: In finding F-01, a polling budget gave better p99 per poll but higher total work.
cases.resolution: The cause is not fully resolved.
